quote: Was bildet bei der Lamé'schen Differentialgl. der Quotient 2er Integrale ab?
english: For the Lamé differential equation, what does the quotient of two integrals map onto?
topic: Hilbert extends an idea from spherical functions (Kugelfunktionen) to algebraic functions, Riemann surfaces, automorphic functions and the Lamé differential equation, and examines the conformal map given by the quotient of two integrals, with a footnote on the inverse of an integral involving $P_n$.

triage.modern_statement: Take the Lamé equation in algebraic form, y'' + ½Σ_{i=1}^{3} y'/(x−e_i) − (n(n+1)x + B)/(4∏(x−e_i)) y = 0. It has regular singular points at e1, e2, e3 and ∞. What is the image of the Schwarz (developing) map s = y1/y2, the ratio of two independent solutions? The standard answer comes from Schwarz–Christoffel/Schwarz-triangle reasoning. When the e_i and the accessory parameter B are real, s maps the upper half-plane conformally onto a circular-arc quadrilateral, which can be read as a spherical quadrilateral. At each finite singular point the exponent difference is 1/2, so those three corners have angle π/2. At ∞ the exponents are −n/2 and (n+1)/2, so the fourth corner has angle (2n+1)π/2. In general, the image is a multivalued map whose monodromy group acts on the sphere. Asking when this group is discrete links the question to automorphic functions and uniformization, which is the setting Hilbert mentions on the page.
triage.answered_by: The general principle that the ratio of two solutions maps the half-plane onto a circular polygon belongs to the Schwarz/Klein school of the 1870s–1890s. Klein wrote papers on Lamé functions in Mathematische Annalen in the 1890s. Fricke studied circular-arc quadrilaterals ('Die Kreisbogenvierseite und das Princip der Symmetrie', Math. Ann. 44, 1894). The modern, complete treatment is by A. Eremenko and A. Gabrielov: 'Spherical rectangles', Arnold Math. J. 2 (2016), 463–486, and 'Moduli spaces for Lamé functions and Abelian integrals of the second kind'. They study spherical quadrilaterals whose angles are odd multiples of π/2 and treat this as equivalent to the accessory-parameter problem for Heun/Lamé equations. I did not open Klein's or Fricke's papers, so I cannot say exactly what each one proves.

evidence.claim: If the singular points, exponents and accessory parameters are real, the ratio of two linearly independent solutions of a Heun-type equation maps the upper half-plane onto a circular polygon. Conversely, every such circular polygon arises from such an equation.

Eremenko and Gabrielov study spherical quadrilaterals whose angles are odd multiples of π/2 and the equivalent accessory-parameter problem for the Heun equation. These are the image polygons of the Lamé Schwarz map.

Eremenko and Gabrielov have a paper titled 'Moduli spaces for Lamé functions and Abelian integrals of the second kind', and they published 'Spherical rectangles' in Arnold Math. Journal 2 (2016), 463–486.

The EUDML reference list for 'Fonctions de Lamé et fonctions de Mathieu' includes Klein's 'Ueber den Hermiteschen Fall der Lameschen Differentialgleichung' (Math. Ann. 40, 1892) and Klein's 'Über Lamé'sche Funktionen'.
Fricke studied circular-arc quadrilaterals in 'Die Kreisbogenvierseite und das Princip der Symmetrie', Math. Ann. 44 (1894), 565–599.

triage.why: Hilbert's note asks a standard question in Schwarz–Klein theory: what is the image of the Schwarz map of the Lamé equation? Classical theory answers it. In the real case the image is a circular-arc (spherical) quadrilateral with three right angles and one angle of (2n+1)π/2. The question is not one of Hilbert's published problems. The detailed classification of these quadrilaterals is a current research topic. Eremenko–Gabrielov and others work on it in connection with Lamé/Heun accessory parameters, metrics of constant curvature with conic singularities, and Painlevé VI. Confidence is medium because the search tool's usage limit stopped me from searching further. I checked the modern sources, but not the exact content of the classical Klein and Fricke papers.
